analysis.one_liner: Requires hospitals and clinics to use needles that retract or shield after use, protecting workers from infection.
analysis.headline: Introduced in May 1999 with 7 Senate backers, the bill never got a committee vote and died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have directed OSHA to rewrite its bloodborne pathogens standard so employers must use needleless systems and needles with built-in safety shields, and it would have required front-line health workers to help pick which devices are used. It also ordered a national database of safer needle devices, a national tally of needlestick injuries, and a rule binding Medicare-participating hospitals that are otherwise exempt from OSHA. The bill was referred to the Senate labor committee and was never brought up again.
analysis.who_benefits: Nurses, aides, technicians, and other direct-care workers who face daily risk of being stuck by a contaminated needle and possibly contracting HIV, hepatitis B, or hepatitis C. Front-line workers also gain a voice in selecting safer devices, and patient safety improves when fewer exposed needles circulate.

how_it_helps.text: Requires employers to use needleless systems and sharps with engineered injury protections wherever they promote employee safety and do not interfere with patient care [S2][S3]
Requires non-managerial direct-care workers to participate in identifying and evaluating the safer devices their workplace adopts [S2][S3]
Mandates a detailed sharps injury log and training for every direct-care worker on each device they use [S2][S3]
Directs NIOSH to build a national database of safer devices, evaluation criteria, a model training curriculum, and a national system collecting comprehensive needlestick injury data [S2][S3]
Closes an OSHA coverage gap by making compliance a condition of Medicare participation for hospitals otherwise exempt from OSHA regulation [S2][S3]

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals, clinics, and other health employers, who must buy safer needle devices, keep extra injury logs, and provide device-specific training. Some of those costs could pass through to insurers and patients.

drawbacks.text: Safer needle devices and needleless systems cost more than conventional needles, and hospitals — especially small and rural ones — would bear the purchasing, logging, and training costs [S3]

Safety mechanisms can interfere with some medical procedures, which the bill itself acknowledges by allowing an employer exemption where the devices do not promote safety or interfere with patient safety or a procedure's success, or are not commercially available [S3]
The sharps injury log requires detailed incident reporting, adding a paperwork burden on top of existing OSHA recordkeeping [S2][S3]
Extending the rules to OSHA-exempt hospitals through Medicare conditions of participation adds federal oversight for facilities that previously fell outside OSHA's reach [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protection is significant: a needlestick can mean a lifetime of testing, prophylactic drugs, and the fear of HIV or hepatitis infection for a nurse or aide, and the bill's own design lets employers seek exemptions where a device genuinely interferes with care. The main honest objection is cost — safer devices and new recordkeeping are more expensive than conventional needles — and the bill does not provide funding to hospitals, authorizing money only for NIOSH's database and training work [S3].

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the Senate labor committee the day it was introduced, the committee never held a vote on it, and it expired when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Barbara Boxer introduced the bill in the Senate on May 26, 1999, with Harry Reid as an original cosponsor [S1][S3][S5]
Six Democratic senators cosponsored the bill, all from the same party as the sponsor [S4]
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on the day of introduction [S5]
The only action after referral was a 'star print' order on July 21, 1999 — a routine reprint request; no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever followed [S5]
The 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001, without the bill ever advancing, so it died in committee [S1][S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals and other health employers came out ahead in the short run, because no federal mandate ever required them to buy safer devices or keep the new injury logs during that Congress. Conventional needle and syringe makers also kept their existing market.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hospitals that faced no device mandate

for.name: Harry Reid
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction, according to the Senate sponsor line [S3]

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions

against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote — for the rest of the Congress [S5]

against.name: Jim Jeffords
against.what_they_did: As committee chairman, never scheduled the bill for a markup or vote during the 106th Congress

sides.party_line_note: All 7 Senate backers — the sponsor and 6 cosponsors — were Democrats, and no Republican signed on; the bill never reached the floor, so there is no vote record to show whether anyone would have opposed it.

industries.note: A federal mandate to use needleless systems and self-shielding needles would create a guaranteed market for their products. In this case the industry's gain and the workers' gain run together: the devices exist to prevent infections.

industries.industry: Hospitals and other health care employers
industries.note: They would bear the cost of buying safer devices, keeping sharps injury logs, and training staff, with no funding provided for compliance. Their financial interest in avoiding the mandate runs against the workers the bill protects.
Devices that do not use needles, and needles with built-in protections, would displace standard products wherever the mandate applies.
